evidence: CDIAL 6152 danta explicitly gives Khowar don tooth, plus widespread dand/dā̃t. The generic Khowar donor-category node found by search is not a competing lexical etymon. Non-Khowar dot/dad shapes are compared with the danta family while vowel and nasal-loss details remain qualified.

CDIAL 11625 vikāla explicitly gives Gawarbati yel night and Torwali byäl, Chiliss biyāli and Shina byāle yesterday. Bashkarik/Bateri biāl fits the same regional yesterday family; the article also has Bashkarik žāl and leaves regional transmission open.
CDIAL 10877.2 *lakkha explicitly gives Maiyan lakh small, younger. The aspirated survey form selects section 2, not *lakka in section 1.
CDIAL 3849 khalla gives Awadhi khāle below and Marathi khāl below. The survey adverbs match section 1, not the khāla drain/channel or khala hollow branches.
CDIAL 2095.2 indūra gives Bengali ĩdur and Assamese endur rat. These eastern idur forms select the i-initial branch; the absence of a nasalization mark is retained in the source record.
CDIAL 13276 sarva explicitly gives Bengali sab all. Survey śob/ʃɔb is the Bengali pronunciation of that form, preserving the source sibilant and vowel.
CDIAL 5155 jala explicitly gives Hindi jal and Gujarati jaḷ water. Mewari jal/jaḷ directly matches; Bagheli jel is compared in the same family with its raised vowel retained as a regional variation.

CDIAL 10816 retra gives Kumaoni reto, Gujarati ret/retī and Old Marwari reta sand. Survey retu/reto/rethi fits that sand family, with aspiration in rethi retained as an unresolved phonetic detail. Turner notes the limited evidence for the reconstructed tr cluster.

CDIAL 12918 saṃdhyā gives Gujarati sā̃j and Marathi sā̃j(h) evening. Nimadi sānjā and Bhil hānj are compared jointly in that evening family; initial h in the Bhil forms is a working regional s/h correspondence. The combined evening/afternoon survey gloss is preserved.

CDIAL 4386 *grilla explicitly gives Punjabi gillā and Hindi gillā wet. The geminate-l forms directly match this family; Turner calls its derivation from *gṛdla very doubtful, a qualification retained here.

CDIAL 10648 raśmi gives Punjabi rassī/rassā rope, a family transmitted into several Indo-Aryan languages, and Western Pahari rośśo rope. The survey rasso/rośi shapes match these regional variants; the precise intra-Indo-Aryan borrowing route remains open.
CDIAL 3049 kāya means body, with Pali/Prakrit kāya. The conservative survey kaya body is linked to this whole noun without asserting a settled learned-versus-inherited route.
CDIAL 12575 śūla explicitly gives Punjabi sūl thorn, spike. Kaithal sul thorn matches that specific sense rather than merely the related pain or impaling-stake senses.

CDIAL 13846 sphuṇṭati/sphuṇḍate gives Bashkarik phuṇḍ flower, Chiliss phundo and Shina phuṇu. These Kohistani phūṇ/phū̃ṇḍ forms fit the documented nasal flower family; the deeper verbal-root alternative remains qualified.
